description: How eight actors become elephants, trains and crowds through physical theatre and narration.
content_html:
The Challenge: One World, Eight Actors

Laura Eason’s stage adaptation of Jules Verne’s novel asks a small ensemble to create an entire planet. Fogg’s journey crosses three continents, dozens of locations, and involves dozens of incidental characters — customs officials, ship’s captains, train conductors, Yokohama acrobats and one very large elephant. With a cast of typically eight, every performer must be skilled in multi-roling: stepping out of a minor part, shedding an accent or a hat, and stepping instantly into another. The play’s pleasure lies in watching this transformation happen live, in front of the audience, with no apology and no disguise.

Understanding these dramatic methods is essential for exam-style questions. Examiners want to see that you recognise why Eason chose this form, not just that the cast is small. The form makes the world feel vast and the journey feel kinetic — qualities a naturalistic production with a large cast and scene-changes could never achieve.

Key Fact

Eason’s adaptation uses multi-roling, mime, direct address narration, object transformation and ensemble physical theatre as its core dramatic methods. Together they let eight actors tell a story that spans the globe.

Narration and Direct Address

One of the production’s most important tools is direct address. Company members step forward to narrate transitions between scenes, update the audience on the days remaining, or comment on Fogg’s progress. This has two effects: it keeps the racing pace alive (no long scene-change during which energy drains away), and it recruits the audience as fellow travellers tracking the wager in real time.

Narration here is not passive. A performer narrating a train journey is also simultaneously performing it — their voice creates the soundscape while their body mimes the carriage, so the boundaries between “telling” and “showing” dissolve. This is ensemble storytelling at its most efficient. The technique owes a debt to practitioners such as Complicite, whose work since the 1980s has made the narrator—performer a central figure in physical theatre.

A common student error is to treat Eason’s ensemble form as a practical limitation — “there aren’t enough actors for a big cast.” This misses the point entirely. Eason chose this form deliberately because the experience of watching actors transform — from a train conductor to an elephant’s front legs to a Reform Club gentleman — creates theatrical energy that a naturalistic production cannot. The rapid role-switching mirrors the dizzying speed of Fogg’s journey. Examiners reward students who understand that the form is the meaning.

Mime and Physical Theatre

Mime is the engine of the production’s scene-setting. Where a naturalistic production would build a set, this company uses bodies. In the journey through India on elephant-back, the ensemble arranges itself to suggest the rhythm and sway of a large animal — one or two performers may form the front legs, others the haunches, while Fogg and Passepartout “ride” on top. The physical precision demanded of the company is equivalent to that of a dance piece.

Similarly, the crossing of the snowy American plains by train sees the ensemble arranged in rows of chairs, collectively swaying as the “carriage” accelerates. A performer at the front enacts the engine’s motion. The audience reads these configurations instantly. The vocabulary draws on the physical theatre tradition associated with Frantic Assembly and Complicite: the body is a flexible instrument capable of representing any object or environment with the right training and ensemble trust.

Key Fact

In this play, mime is not a fallback for missing props — it is the primary visual language. The audience’s imagination is recruited as a co-creator: they read a row of sway-and-jostle bodies as a train because the physical rhythm is unmistakably right.

Object Transformation

Object transformation is the third pillar of this production’s method. Chairs become railway carriages or the pews of a Reform Club; a length of rope becomes the rigging of a ship; a cane becomes a walking stick and then a conductor’s baton and then a rifle. The audience learns to interpret these transformations rapidly, partly because the physical use of the object teaches them what it “is” at any given moment.

This technique demands that performers commit fully. A chair is only a railway carriage if the performer sitting in it behaves exactly as they would in a moving train. The physical life — the sway, the grip on an imaginary armrest, the gaze out of an invisible window — persuades the audience. Break the physical logic and the fiction collapses. This requirement for total physical commitment is a core principle of physical theatre.

As a performer playing one of the ensemble in the elephant sequence, you might hold a low-to-the-ground posture, knees slightly bent, arms loose at the sides to suggest bulk. Your rhythm would synchronise with the other “legs” of the elephant — a slow, deliberate, four-count sway. Vocally, you would be silent: the physical work carries the scene. Your proxemics to the other ensemble members are tight — within touching distance — to suggest you are one creature rather than separate performers.

As a lighting designer, you might use a warm amber lighting special from a high angle to suggest the heat of the Indian sun. A gobo projecting dappled leaf-shadow patterns could suggest jungle canopy without a single physical piece of set. The warm wash would contrast with the cooler, greyer light used in London, immediately orientating the audience in a different part of the world.

Fast Costume Changes and Comic Timing

Multi-roling also demands a distinctive costume strategy. The production typically uses a base layer for each performer — a neutral Victorian suit or simple rehearsal costume — onto which accessories are layered rapidly: a hat, a badge, an accent, a way of walking. The base layer plus accessories system means a change from Reform Club gentleman to Indian customs official takes seconds rather than minutes.

Alongside this runs one of the production’s most important performance demands: comic timing. The play’s humour depends on the contrast between Fogg’s absolute stillness — his refusal to be rattled by any obstacle — and Passepartout’s physical and emotional expressiveness. Fogg’s stillness is the comic engine: it sets up a straight line against which Passepartout’s energy lands. Examiners reward students who understand that Fogg’s restraint is as much a performance choice as Passepartout’s flamboyance.
exam_tip_html: When you are asked to analyse intentions for a 12-mark question on this play, the most common error is to describe what happens rather than analysing why Eason chose this dramatic method and what effect it creates for the audience. Ask yourself: what does multi-roling make the audience feel? (Excitement, a sense of the world’s variety, admiration for the company.) What would be lost if a naturalistic cast played each character? (Speed, the theatrical pleasure of transformation, the sense that the play celebrates the act of storytelling itself.) Pin every point to a specific moment and a specific effect on the audience.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Multi-roling, mime, direct address narration and object transformation are Eason’s core dramatic methods — they allow eight performers to create a globe-spanning world and are central to the play’s theatrical identity.
  • Narration collapses the boundary between telling and showing: the narrating performer is simultaneously performing the action, keeping pace alive and recruiting the audience as fellow travellers.
  • Comic timing — particularly the contrast between Fogg’s stillness and Passepartout’s energy — is a performance choice, not an accident; examiners reward students who analyse it as a deliberate method with a specific effect on the audience.

practice_questions.text: Name the dramatic method in which one actor plays more than one character during a performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: multi-roling (accept multi-role playing or role-doubling).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'direct address' as used in theatrical performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that direct address involves the performer speaking to the audience; 1 mark for explaining that it breaks or acknowledges the fourth wall, stepping outside the dramatic fiction.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Eason uses mime to create the sense of an elephant in this play. Refer to specific physical choices the ensemble might make.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of mime as a technique (1); explanation of specific physical choices (low posture, synchronised rhythm, collective sway) (1); reference to the specific moment of the Indian journey (1); analysis of the effect on the audience (creates the creature through imagination, demonstrates physical theatre skill, makes the transformation visible and exciting) (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of the base-layer-plus-accessories costume strategy on the audience during rapid multi-roling transitions. Give a specific example from the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming the costume strategy and how it works (1); a specific example of a role transition in the play (e.g. Reform Club gentleman to customs official) (1); explanation of the effect on pace (transitions are instant, energy is maintained) (1); explanation of the effect on the audience (sense of theatrical magic, admiration for skill, delight in the visible act of transformation) (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in using narration and direct address throughout the play. What is the audience meant to understand about their role in the storytelling?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full analysis of Eason's intentions across multiple narrative functions of direct address. Identifies that the audience is consciously recruited as a fellow traveller; that narration replaces scene-change transitions to maintain pace; that the technique self-reflexively celebrates storytelling as a theatrical act. Every point anchored to a named moment of the play with a named effect on audience understanding or emotion. Awareness of the Complicite/physical-theatre tradition behind this technique.

Secure: Identifies at least two purposes of narration and direct address with generally accurate effect on audience. At least one named moment. Some awareness of the theatrical tradition.

Developing: Identifies that direct address breaks the fourth wall and that narration updates the audience on the journey. Generic effect stated rather than analysed. Little reference to specific moments.

Emerging: Basic description of what narration does (tells the audience what is happening). No analysis of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would stage the moment when the ensemble represents a moving train during the crossing of the American plains. Discuss set, lighting, sound and performer choices you would make, and explain the effect of each choice on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision integrating set, lighting, sound and performer choices, all anchored to this specific moment. Set: specific use of chairs arranged in rows, minimal additional furniture, positioning on stage (upstage to downstage for sense of travel). Lighting: choice of lantern type and colour to suggest landscape (cool, wide wash; possible gobo for prairie light), transition cues as the train accelerates. Sound: specific soundscape elements named (steam whistle, rhythmic wheel click, wind, the attack sequence building from distance). Performer: specific physical vocabulary for collective sway, synchronised arm-and-body rhythms, the stillness of Fogg against the animated ensemble. Every choice is given a named effect on the audience. Substantiated directorial judgement about the overall intended experience.

Secure: Most design disciplines covered, generally concrete choices. At least one named design element and one performer choice with effects. The moment is correctly identified and the staging is coherent.

Developing: Some design disciplines covered but choices are generic (e.g. 'exciting lighting', 'train sound effects'). Effects are implied rather than stated. Limited performer detail.

Emerging: Basic listing of design ideas with little or no effect. Largely descriptive rather than directorial.

knowledge_checks.q: Which technique involves one actor playing more than one character in the same production?
In Around the World in 80 Days, what is the primary purpose of direct address narration?
options: To explain the plot to a confused audience
To maintain pace and recruit the audience as fellow travellers tracking the wager
To allow the playwright to voice their personal opinions
To replace the costume designer's work

knowledge_checks.q: The technique in which a chair becomes a train carriage or a rope becomes ship rigging is called _____ transformation.
Fogg's _____ on stage creates the comic engine that allows Passepartout's energy to land effectively.
Match each dramatic method to its key function in this production.
right: Allows one actor to play dozens of incidental characters across the globe
Lets the company create animals and vehicles using only their bodies
Converts simple props into trains, ships and elephants without scene changes

flashcard_questions.a: One actor playing more than one character during a performance.

flashcard_questions.q: What is direct address in theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: A performer speaks directly to the audience, breaking the fourth wall.
A company builds a story through shared physical action, narration and group work.
Using a simple prop to represent multiple different objects across a performance.
Performance without words where the body communicates action and environment.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the base layer plus accessories costume system?
flashcard_questions.a: Performers wear a neutral outfit and add items to signal rapid character changes.
The precise use of pause and rhythm to land a joke at maximum impact.

Where did the stage adaptation of Around the World in 80 Days premiere?

The physical distance between performers on stage, signalling relationship and emotion.

flashcard_questions.a: His refusal to react sets up a straight line against which Passepartout's energy lands.

What is a gobo in lighting design?
flashcard_questions.a: A plate placed in front of a lantern to project a pattern onto the stage.

glossary_terms.definition: The theatrical technique in which one actor plays more than one character, switching between roles during a performance.
A technique in which a performer speaks directly to the audience, breaking the imaginary fourth wall of the play.
Theatre in which the company collaboratively builds a story through physical action, narration and ensemble work rather than realistic staging.
Performance without words in which the body communicates action, character and environment.
A staging technique in which a simple prop or piece of furniture is used to represent multiple different objects during a performance, often in different scenes.
A performance style in which the body, rather than text or set, is the primary means of creating meaning, often involving stylised movement, acrobatics and ensemble precision.
The physical distance between performers on stage, used to signal relationships, status and emotion.
A specific lighting state focused on one part of the stage, often created by a profile lantern, to isolate a character or moment.
A metal or glass plate placed in front of a lantern to project a pattern or shape onto the stage.
A costume approach in which performers wear a neutral outfit throughout and add or remove items to signal character changes.
The precise control of pause, rhythm and speed in delivery or movement to create maximum comedic impact.
